spec.theme: preserving a night market's character during redevelopment

blueprint.speaker: Teodora Vask, a writer who grew up working at her aunt's fried-noodle stall in the Halvern Street night market in the fictional port city of Orrisport
blueprint.audience: Members of the Orrisport Redevelopment Council and civically engaged residents reading the local journal during the public comment period on the market plan
blueprint.exigence: The Council has published a redevelopment plan that would replace the market's self-built stalls with a covered pavilion of sixty identical stalls and a 'curated vendor mix'; the comment period closes at the end of the month
blueprint.purpose: To persuade the Council to amend the plan so that it fixes safety hazards while leaving the stalls, vendor tenure, and informal customs intact
blueprint.context: A sixty-year-old informal night market that grew out of after-dark fish sales in the 1950s; a nearby market, Marrow Lane, was standardized in 2009 and lost its vendors and late hours
blueprint.claim: A market's character is not a look that can be designed but a set of habits held by particular people over a long time; a plan that standardizes stalls and reselects vendors will destroy what it claims to preserve, so the Council should repair hazards and leave the rest alone
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with an anecdote of a blackout in which unorganized vendors lit lanterns in unison (par. 1), then traces the market's unplanned accretion (par. 2); summarizes the plan and concedes the safety problems are real before showing the plan goes far beyond safety (par. 3); offers Marrow Lane as a nearby precedent of the same approach failing (par. 4); defines character as habits rather than appearance, which explains why the precedent failed (par. 5); closes with a concrete alternative and direct appeal to the Council (par. 6)
evidence_types: numerical details (sixty stalls, a third of vendors, eighteen months vs. sixty years)

devices.function: Opens with the 1987 blackout to dramatize spontaneous, unorganized coordination before the plan is introduced
Lanterns 'like a procession that had decided to stand still' conveys collective, unplanned unity
Two very short sentences after a long one emphasize that no one organized the lanterns
After 'Nobody organized that,' the plan is 'above all, organized,' turning the Council's virtue into the problem
Traces how fish sales led to food stalls, then to a system of inherited spots, showing accretion rather than design
Sixty stalls, a third of vendors leaving, eighteen months versus sixty years give the argument concrete scale
Grants that the wiring is dangerous, then pivots to the plan's overreach in selecting vendors and raising rents
Marrow Lane's ordinance closing at nine is set against Halvern Street's closing 'when the last cook is too tired'
Redefines 'character' as habits held by people over time rather than a visual style
'You can photograph the sailcloth. You cannot photograph the tolerance.' sharpens the look-versus-habit distinction
Parallel 'that' clauses enumerate specific habits; parallel imperatives lay out the alternative plan
Colons introduce lists that concretize abstractions (the plan's features, the Council's idea of character, the habits)
'None of this means the market should stay dangerous' limits the claim before the proposal
Addresses Council members directly with the deadline and a final charge
Knowing 'where the lanterns are' stands for the accumulated local knowledge the plan would discard

blueprint.counterargument: The Council's position that the market is hazardous and needs modern infrastructure; the writer concedes the wiring and drainage problems fully but argues the plan goes beyond safety into vendor selection, lotteries, and rents that will destroy the habits that constitute character

provenance.note: Original essay written for this practice set; all people, places, and figures are fictional.

set.title: Where the Lanterns Are
paragraphs: On the night in 1987 when the power failed along Halvern Street, my aunt Ines kept frying.

She had a camping lantern under the counter, a habit from the years before the market had any wiring at all, and within ten minutes every stall on the block was lit the same way, forty small flames in a row like a procession that had decided to stand still.
Nobody organized that.
Nobody could have.
I think of those lanterns now because the Orrisport Redevelopment Council has published its plan for the market, and the plan is, above all, organized.
The Halvern Street market was never founded; it accumulated.
In the early 1950s, fishmongers from the quay began selling the day's unsold catch from handcarts after dark, and the people who bought from them wanted something to eat while they waited.
A woman named Pell Orano set a griddle on a crate.

Within a decade there were stalls built from salvaged doors, awnings stitched from sailcloth, and an unwritten system of rights by which a family's spot passed from parent to child without anyone ever signing a lease.
The city tolerated it, taxed it lightly, and for sixty years mostly left it alone.
The Council's plan would replace all of this with a covered pavilion of sixty identical stalls, a central payment kiosk, and what the document calls a "curated vendor mix."
I want to be fair to the people who wrote it.
The wiring on Halvern Street is a genuine hazard; I have seen extension cords running through puddles, and the drainage has not been improved since my aunt's time.
A market that electrocutes its customers has no character worth defending.
But the plan does not stop at the wiring.
It proposes to select which vendors return, to assign their positions by lottery, and to charge rents that the document itself admits will be "substantially above current informal levels."
We have seen this before, two miles away.
The Marrow Lane market was rebuilt in 2009 along almost exactly these lines: a handsome steel roof, uniform counters, a selection committee.
The ribbon was cut in May.

By the following winter, a third of the chosen vendors had given up their leases, the committee had filled the gaps with a coffee franchise and a shop selling scented candles, and the market closed, by ordinance, at nine o'clock.
Halvern Street does not close at nine.
It closes when the last cook is too tired to stand, which is a different kind of rule, and one no committee has ever managed to write down.
What the Council means by character, I suspect, is a look: the lanterns, the sailcloth, the handwritten signs that its renderings reproduce so lovingly.
But character, in a market, is not a look.

It is a set of habits held by particular people over a long time: the knowledge that Orano's grandson will take the corner because his grandmother took it, that a new vendor earns a spot by being tolerated at the edges for a season, that a dispute about a spilled bucket is settled by the oldest woman on the block and not by a kiosk.
You can photograph the sailcloth.
You cannot photograph the tolerance.
A pavilion can be built in eighteen months; the habits took sixty years, and they are not transferable to whoever wins a lottery.
None of this means the market should stay dangerous.
Fix the wiring; the vendors have asked for it since before I was born.
Lay proper drains.

Then leave the stalls where they are, grant the existing families the tenure they have always held in practice, and let the edges stay ragged enough for the next Pell Orano to set a griddle on a crate.
Council members, you have until the end of the month to amend this plan.
You can give Halvern Street a roof.
Make sure that when the lights go out beneath it, there is still someone who knows where the lanterns are.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer's admission that the wiring is "a genuine hazard" most likely matters to the Council members in her audience because it

options.text: signals that she accepts the pavilion, the kiosk, and the vendor lottery as reasonable responses to the drainage and electrical problems
options.label: reversal
options.why: The very next sentences reject the vendor selection, lottery, and rents as going beyond the wiring; she accepts the safety repairs, not the pavilion's other features.

options.text: reminds them that the vendors, not the city, are responsible for the extension cords running through the puddles
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never assigns blame to vendors; paragraph 6 notes the vendors have asked for repairs 'since before I was born,' which if anything implies the city neglected them.

options.text: shows that she shares their safety concerns, so her objections cannot be dismissed as resistance to any change at all
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer explicitly says 'I want to be fair to the people who wrote it' and grants the hazard fully, which positions her later objection (sentences 15-16) as targeted at overreach rather than at the idea of improvement; this credibility matters to officials who might otherwise label her nostalgic.

options.text: persuades them that the market's safety problems are minor compared with the cultural loss the plan would cause
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: She calls the hazard 'genuine' and says a market that electrocutes customers has no character worth defending; the concession does not minimize safety but affirms it.

items.stem: The account of the Marrow Lane market in paragraph 4 is most clearly designed to appeal to the audience's

options.text: belief that city governments should never regulate the operating hours of privately run markets
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer contrasts the nine o'clock ordinance with Halvern Street's custom, but she never argues against regulation in general; paragraph 6 asks the city to act on wiring and drains.

options.text: distaste for coffee franchises and candle shops as businesses unworthy of a traditional market setting
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The franchise and candle shop are details illustrating what replaced departed vendors; the appeal rests on the overall collapse of the rebuilt market, not on hostility to particular businesses.

options.text: fondness for the steel roof and uniform counters that made the rebuilt market handsome
options.label: reversal
options.why: 'Handsome' is used wryly; the paragraph presents the roof and uniform counters as features of a plan that failed, not as attractions the audience should want.

options.text: reluctance to repeat a visible local failure of public investment that is only two miles away
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens 'We have seen this before, two miles away' and details how a plan 'along almost exactly these lines' lost a third of its vendors within a year, inviting council members and residents to recognize a precedent they already know.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 2 within the passage as a whole?

options.text: It introduces Pell Orano as the founder whose family should be given final authority over which vendors are selected
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Orano appears as one example of spontaneous beginnings, and the paragraph explicitly says the market was 'never founded'; nothing proposes giving her family authority.

options.text: It provides the history of the market's unplanned growth, laying the groundwork for the later definition of character as accumulated habit
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 2 traces accretion ('never founded; it accumulated,' inherited spots without leases) that paragraph 5 later names as the habits constituting character; the history makes the definition credible.

options.text: It argues that the city's long neglect of the market is the real cause of the wiring and drainage hazards the Council now cites
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph says the city 'mostly left it alone' as a neutral fact; it does not connect that neglect to the hazards, which are raised in paragraph 3 without blame.

options.text: It contrasts the market's early fish trade with its present food stalls to show how far the market has drifted from its origins
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The paragraph presents fish sales leading naturally to food stalls as continuity, not drift; the writer's point is accumulation, not loss of original purpose.

items.stem: The placement of the sentence "But the plan does not stop at the wiring" in paragraph 3 is effective primarily because it

options.text: withdraws the writer's earlier admission that the extension cords and drainage pose a serious danger to customers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence does not retract the concession; the wiring remains a 'genuine hazard' that paragraph 6 again insists must be fixed.

options.text: introduces the Marrow Lane comparison that the writer develops across the remainder of the paragraph
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Marrow Lane is introduced in paragraph 4, not in the rest of paragraph 3, which instead lists the plan's provisions.

options.text: summarizes the plan's three main provisions before the writer evaluates each one in turn over the next paragraphs
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence is a pivot, not a summary; the provisions are listed in the sentence that follows it, and the later paragraphs do not evaluate them one by one.

options.text: limits the preceding concession and redirects the paragraph toward the features of the plan the writer actually opposes
options.label: correct
options.why: Coming right after the writer grants the hazard and admits a dangerous market has no character worth defending, the short sentence marks the boundary of her agreement and sets up the list of vendor selection, lottery, and rents in sentence 16.

items.stem: Taken together, the details of the passage suggest that the writer is responding most directly to which of the following situations?

options.text: The failure of the Marrow Lane market, which has prompted the city to reconsider covered pavilions
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Marrow Lane is offered by the writer as a cautionary precedent in paragraph 4; nothing suggests the city is reconsidering anything because of it.

options.text: The announced closing of the market's original stalls, which the writer hopes to delay
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The plan would replace the stalls, but it has not been finalized or scheduled; the writer seeks amendment of a proposal, not a delay of an announced closing.

options.text: A recent electrical accident at the market that has renewed calls for the stalls to be rewired
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer calls the wiring a hazard and mentions cords in puddles, but no accident is described; the hazard is background, not the triggering event.

options.text: A published redevelopment plan that is still open to amendment for a limited period
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 states the Council 'has published its plan,' and paragraph 6 tells Council members they 'have until the end of the month to amend this plan,' establishing a plan under public review as the occasion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the writer's stance toward the Council's plan as a whole?

options.text: Resigned acceptance that the market's customs will vanish however the plan is revised
